analysis:
Examined ProviderLoop+Lifecycle.swift (head 100-116) and the two test files.

The only production change is in performLifecycleDrain. A graceful drain used to require a coordinator drain acknowledgement (or no client). It now also settles when the client has no registered connection (`coordinatorSettled = acknowledged || coordinatorClient == nil || !hasRegisteredConnection()`). Every other drain condition is unchanged: nativeOwnersDrained, lifecycleRemaining == 0, and the App Attest worker retired via stopAppAttestWorkerAndWait. A forced drain is unchanged. The drain exit also sets lifecycleStatus.coordinatorAcknowledged only from the real ack, so telemetry stays honest.

Security relevance: this does not weaken admission control, serving authorization (A-016, T-053), or encryption. servingDrain.drained() is reached only after accepted work (lifecycleRemaining) has finished and the worker is retired, so no in-flight consumer data is truncated. Without a registered session the coordinator has no live connection to the provider; the in-code comment says a disconnect already cancelled accepted work. I could not verify that comment from the supplied source. The accepted-work count is still checked by lifecycleRemaining, so any leftover work still blocks the drain.

The remaining unverified contract is how hasRegisteredConnection() is defined. If it can return false during a transient reconnect while a session is still live on a socket not yet marked registered, a drain could finish without the FIFO ack. The effect would be a possibly lost final usage message or terminal (billing/availability), not a confidentiality issue. I saw no evidence of this, so I record it rather than report a finding.

The handshake-deadline test file references CoordinatorConnectionHandshake, CoordinatorError.handshakeTimeout and CoordinatorClientConfig.handshakeTimeout. Those production sources are not in this batch. A timeout that cancels a stalled connection is a defensive availability gain (T-010, TB-002) and the test-only loopback listener is not new attack surface. The tests I reviewed introduce no secrets.
